entities.name: Tashedkhonsu
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Tashedkhonsu, a royal woman of the early Twenty-second Dynasty of ancient Egypt (c. 945–715 BCE), served as a principal wife of Pharaoh Osorkon I and, crucially, as the mother of Pharaoh Takelot I. Her significance, though primarily attested through a single monumental inscription, lies in her pivotal genealogical position within a period marked by the consolidation of Libyan rule in Egypt. Bearing the esteemed title 'God's Mother' on the Pasenhor stela, she embodied the symbolic and political power wielded by royal women in legitimizing the succession during a complex era of dynastic shifts and co-regencies. Her existence provides a vital link in the understanding of the royal lineage that governed from Tanis.

The primary evidence for Tashedkhonsu's life comes from the aforementioned Pasenhor stela, dated to the reign of Shoshenq V, a later ruler of the 22nd Dynasty. This stela, a genealogical record, explicitly names her as the mother of Takelot I, solidifying her status within the royal family tree. Furthermore, a shabti figurine inscribed with her name was discovered in the tomb of Takelot II at Tanis, a pharaoh who ruled significantly later. This unexpected find suggests a posthumous reverence or a deliberate inclusion of an important ancestor's funerary object in a descendant's burial, hinting at her enduring, if understated, importance within the royal memory. Such archaeological evidence, however scarce, allows historians to reconstruct the intricate familial connections that underpinned pharaonic power.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Tashedkhonsu's role as mother to Pharaoh Takelot I provided a direct and essential link in the royal succession of the Twenty-second Dynasty, contributing to the stability and legitimacy of Libyan rule in Egypt for generations. Her mention on the Pasenhor stela and the discovery of her shabti offer critical, albeit rare, insights into the genealogical structure and posthumous veneration within this period.
